passage:
Ishita ran the project team like a tight ship. She read every message aloud and corrected slides in front of everyone. “That's not how we do it. Do it again.” Gurleen used to bring three ideas to each meeting. In the first month one was called silly. By the third month Gurleen brought none. Gurleen nodded, said “sure,” typed what was asked and left at exactly six.

On Friday a teammate asked, “You okay?” “Yeah, just busy,” said Gurleen. Walking home, Gurleen realised the excitement that used to make ideas fizz had gone flat. The work was done and correct. Nobody asked what Gurleen thought, and Gurleen had stopped wanting to say.

qa.q: How many ideas did Gurleen bring to each meeting at first?
qa.a: Gurleen used to bring three ideas to each meeting.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen say “Yeah, just busy” to the teammate?
qa.a: Gurleen felt drained and did not want to explain, so hiding the flat motivation seemed easier than risking Ishita's reaction.

qa.q: What small step could Gurleen take next to bring a voice back?
qa.a: Gurleen could send one idea in writing to Ishita or speak with the teammate who asked, and consider telling Ishita privately how the public corrections land.

qa.q: What might the teammate who asked “You okay?” have noticed?
qa.a: The teammate noticed Gurleen had gone quiet, and probably felt the same tension under Ishita and wondered whether to speak up too.

grounding: A team member under a domineering leader feels tense, stops offering ideas and complies outwardly while motivation drains away.

passage:
“We're using my design,” Lalremsiami said, before anyone had sat down. “Tejas, you do the wiring. No changes.”

“Maybe we could test the second circuit too?” Tejas said.

“No. I decided last night.”

“Okay.”

Anil rolled his eyes but said nothing. Mira stared at her laptop.

“Any questions?” Lalremsiami asked.

Silence.

“Good.”

Later, in the corridor, Anil muttered, “I had an idea about the sensor.”

“Why didn't you say it?” Mira asked.

“What's the point?”

Tejas shrugged. “I used to bring ideas. Now I just bring the wiring.”

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami tell Tejas to do?
qa.a: Lalremsiami told Tejas to do the wiring.

qa.q: What does Tejas mean by saying, “Now I just bring the wiring”?
qa.a: Tejas feels motivation draining and has stopped offering ideas, doing only the assigned task.

qa.q: What could Anil have done differently with the sensor idea?
qa.a: Anil could have written the sensor idea down and sent it, or asked the team to hear it, instead of muttering in the corridor.

qa.q: What might Mira be thinking, staring at the laptop?
qa.a: Mira probably feels tense and reluctant to speak, weighing whether an idea is worth the risk of being shut down.

grounding: A team member under an autocratic project leader feels tense and stops offering ideas while complying outwardly.

passage:
Kiran, you think your college team captain is too bossy? Let your Imran mamu tell you about Sharma.
Sharma was our college cricket captain when I was twenty. He decided everything: batting order, field placements, even who could talk at team meetings. If you suggested something, he'd shout, “Who's captain here?”
At first I tried. I told him their spinner was weak against left-handers. He shouted me down in front of the whole team. After that, I stopped suggesting anything. I played, I fielded, I said “Yes, captain.” Inside, I didn't care if we won.
We lost the semi-final. Afterwards, three of us admitted we'd seen the problem coming. None of us had said a word.

qa.q: What did Sharma shout if someone suggested something?
qa.a: He'd shout, "Who's captain here?"

qa.q: How did young Imran feel after being shouted down?
qa.a: He felt tense and discouraged, stopped suggesting anything and no longer cared inside whether they won.

qa.q: At what point in the story could things have gone differently?
qa.a: If Sharma had listened when Imran raised the spinner, or if the players had spoken up together, the team might have kept its ideas.

qa.q: How might the other players have felt under Sharma?
qa.a: They probably felt tense and silenced too, since three of them later admitted seeing the problem but saying nothing.

grounding: An elder recalls a domineering college captain who shouted down ideas, and how he complied outwardly while his motivation drained.

passage:
Twenty-four hours into the hackathon, the team's app still crashed on login, and the judging was at nine a.m. Mridul, the team lead, paced behind their laptops.
“Hafsa, don't touch the backend. Just do what I say.”
Hafsa had an idea about the login bug. She'd noticed it in the first hour. She opened her mouth, then remembered last night, when he'd snapped, “I'll decide what's important.”
She closed her mouth and fixed the buttons he'd asked for.
At four a.m., the others were quiet too, just typing. Nobody joked. Nobody suggested anything.
At nine, the app crashed during the demo. Hafsa stared at the floor. She'd known the fix since the first hour. She just hadn't cared enough to fight any more.

qa.q: When was the judging?
qa.a: At nine a.m.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when she closed her mouth?
qa.a: She felt tense and discouraged, remembering being snapped at, so she stayed silent.

qa.q: What went wrong in the team, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Mridul's orders silenced everyone, so Hafsa's fix was never shared; a lead who asks for ideas, even under pressure, could have saved the demo.

qa.q: How might the other team members have felt at four a.m.?
qa.a: They were probably tired and tense, just typing without joking or suggesting anything, the same way Hafsa felt.

grounding: Shows a team member under an autocratic lead who stops offering ideas, complying outwardly while her motivation drains away.

passage:
At the Chennai college quiz club, Pranav had been president for a month. He picked the questions, the teams, the practice timings. When someone suggested a sports round, he said, “My club, my rules,” and laughed. No one else laughed.
Shalini used to come early and bring new questions she'd found. Now she came five minutes late, sat at the back, answered when asked and left right after.
Her friend Keerthi asked her, “You used to love this. What happened?”
Shalini shrugged. “Whatever I say, he'll do his thing anyway. So why bother?”
She still showed up every Wednesday. She still said “Yes, Pranav.” But she hadn't brought a single new question in three weeks.

qa.q: What did Pranav say when someone suggested a sports round?
qa.a: He said, "My club, my rules."

qa.q: How does Shalini feel about the club now?
qa.a: She feels discouraged and flat, thinking there's no point contributing because Pranav will do his thing anyway.

qa.q: What could Pranav do to bring members back to life?
qa.a: He could ask members to bring and choose questions, and try one suggested round, so people feel their ideas matter.

qa.q: How might Keerthi see the change in Shalini?
qa.a: Keerthi seems surprised and concerned, noticing her friend's lost enthusiasm.

grounding: Shows a club member under an autocratic president who stops offering ideas, complying outwardly while motivation drains.

passage:
"Ayesha, the survey questions. I've rewritten them. Use mine."
"Oh. I'd added two on commute time, because the pilot showed..."
"Not needed. We follow the plan." Mohit tapped the printout. "The report format is mine too. Just fill in the numbers."
Ayesha looked at Ravi and Sana. Ravi was studying his pen. Sana gave a tiny shrug.
"Okay," Ayesha said.
After Mohit left, Sana whispered, "You had a good point about commute time."
"Doesn't matter." Ayesha shut her laptop. "Last month I stayed up doing extra reading for this project. Now I just want to finish my part and go."
"You used to love this stuff."
"I used to think someone wanted my ideas." She packed her bag. "I'll send the numbers by Friday. Exactly his format."

qa.q: What had Ayesha added two questions about?
qa.a: Commute time.

qa.q: How has Ayesha's feeling about the project changed?
qa.a: Ayesha feels deflated and unmotivated; once eager enough to read extra, she now just wants to finish her part and leave.

qa.q: What could the team try so their ideas get heard?
qa.a: Ayesha and Sana could raise the pilot finding together at the next meeting, or ask Mohit to review one suggestion before the plan is fixed.

qa.q: What might Sana be feeling as she watches?
qa.a: Sana seems uncomfortable and sympathetic, agreeing with Ayesha privately but only shrugging in front of Mohit.

grounding: Shows a team member under a domineering leader who stops offering ideas, complying outwardly while motivation drains away.
